The answer is threads. Each processor can run one or more threads simultaneously based on their architecture. All 16 processors share the load of the operating system. The OS schedules tasks to run on threads which get assigned to an available processor core or at least one with less process load. This is how multitasking happens in the OS, but it's more complicated than that really. A highly CPU intensive program can be written to spawn many threads to do work in parallel. These extra cores will give this multithreaded application a great advantage over more common single threaded applications which will only make use of one core. The programmer must take care in the design of the program though to prevent the OS from being overwhelmed by a thread/CPU core hungry app. There is a functional limit to the number of cores that can be employed as the scheduling and even the physical distances between the wiring of more cores becomes a limiting factor in communication efficiency and OS complexity. Sixteen cores is quite reasonable today and it won't be long before this is considered standard on most PCs.
